desc:
Cut the array arr into consecutive non-empty blocks, each of length at most k. Then overwrite every element of a block with the largest value of that block. Return the largest possible sum of the array after this change.

arr = [2,1,3], k = 2  -> 8    (blocks [2] and [1,3] become [2] and [3,3]: 2 + 3 + 3)
arr = [4,4,4], k = 1  -> 12   (every block has length 1, nothing changes)
arr = [1,5,2,2], k = 3 -> 17  (blocks [1,5,2] and [2] become [5,5,5] and [2]: 15 + 2)
hints: Think about the last block of the array. If it has length L, everything before it is a smaller instance of the same question.
Let dp[i] be the best sum for the first i elements. The last block covers positions i-L .. i-1 for some L from 1 to k and contributes L * max(arr[i-L..i-1]).
For each i, walk L from 1 up to min(k, i) and keep a running maximum of the block, so every candidate costs O(1): dp[i] = max(dp[i-L] + L * runningMax).
editorial: Define dp[i] as the maximum sum obtainable from the first i elements, with dp[0] = 0. The block that ends at position i has some length L ≤ k. All its elements become the block maximum, so it adds L * max, and the elements before it are an independent subproblem: dp[i] = max over L of dp[i - L] + L * max(arr[i-L..i-1]).

While L grows by one the block extends one step to the left, so the block maximum can be maintained incrementally instead of recomputed. This gives O(n · k) time and O(n) space. The first element of a block never needs to be small: the dp automatically considers every possible block boundary.
